---
title: "Why use random variables?"
execute:
  enabled: true
  echo: true

The foundations chapter defined [outcomes and sample spaces](../foundations/possibilities-and-events.qmd#membership-and-granularity), [events](../foundations/events.qmd), and [probability measures](../foundations/probability-measures.qmd#the-three-requirements). An outcome in a pronunciation lexicon may be a complete entry containing an orthographic form, a pronunciation variant, and an ordered phone sequence. But a research question may concern only the number of phones. How can we ask a probability question about that number while retaining the complete entry as the outcome?

A random variable resolves this mismatch by mapping a rich outcome to the particular value used in an analysis.

We specify the pronunciation-entry outcomes, map them to phone-count values and their induced events, and then show how one outcome can support several variables without becoming several observations.

## The pronunciation-entry outcomes

We use the [CMU Pronouncing Dictionary (CMUdict) version 0.7b](https://cmusphinx.github.io/2014/11/cmudict-0-7b-update/), a machine-readable pronunciation lexicon for US English developed for speech technology. The source is distributed under CMU's permissive license, and the [prepared pronunciation table](../data/cmudict/cmudict-pronunciations.csv) retains every pronunciation entry and its ARPAbet phone sequence. It then deterministically counts all phones and vowel phones, identifying vowels from CMUdict's stress digits. The [data record](../data/cmudict/README.md) gives the source checksum, preprocessing, and license.

Each row records one dictionary pronunciation. An orthographic form with two
listed pronunciations contributes two related rows, and CMUdict supplies no
frequency with which either pronunciation occurs in speech. Every probability
on this page therefore comes from giving the prepared pronunciation rows equal
weight; speech-token frequencies play no role.

```{r}
#| label: load-cmudict-why
library(ggplot2)

cmu <- read.csv(
  "data/cmudict/cmudict-pronunciations.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  check.names = FALSE,
  na.strings = ""
)
cmu$outcome_id <- seq_len(nrow(cmu))

stopifnot(
  nrow(cmu) == 133854L,
  !anyDuplicated(cmu$entry),
  all(cmu$phone_count >= cmu$vowel_phone_count),
  !anyNA(cmu[c("entry", "phones", "phone_count", "vowel_phone_count")])
)

head(cmu[c("outcome_id", "entry", "phones", "phone_count",
           "vowel_phone_count")])
```

ARPAbet represents an English pronunciation as an ordered sequence of phone
symbols. A digit on a vowel marks lexical stress: `0` is unstressed, `1` has
primary stress, and `2` has secondary stress. Thus the first displayed entry,
`!EXCLAMATION-POINT`, has 15 phones and five vowels in the sequence `EH2 K S K
L AH0 M EY1 SH AH0 N P OY2 N T`. The counts are deterministic summaries of
that sequence; they are not additional pronunciations.

Three units must remain separate. An orthographic word groups entries that
share `word`; a pronunciation entry is one row, including an alternate label
such as `(2)`; and a running-speech token is an occurrence in a corpus. This
table represents pronunciation entries only. Alternate rows for the same word
are thus related outcomes, while token frequency is unavailable.

Let $\Omega$ contain the `r format(nrow(cmu), big.mark = ",")` pronunciation-entry outcomes. Define

$$
X(\omega)\equiv\text{number of phones in pronunciation entry }\omega
$$

and

$$
V(\omega)\equiv\text{number of vowel phones in pronunciation entry }\omega.
$$

The outcome remains the complete entry. The mappings return two numerical properties of that entry.

```{r}
#| label: plot-cmudict-mapping
#| fig-cap: "Observed phone and vowel-phone counts. Point area represents the number of pronunciation entries with each pair of values."
ggplot(cmu, aes(vowel_phone_count, phone_count)) +
  geom_count(color = "grey", fill = "lightgrey") +
  labs(x = "Vowel phones in pronunciation",
       y = "All phones in pronunciation",
       size = "Entries") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## Values give us new events

We derive a threshold from the empirical phone-count distribution rather than choosing a convenient number.

```{r}
#| label: cmudict-value-event
phone_threshold <- unname(quantile(cmu$phone_count, 0.75, type = 1))
long_entries <- cmu$outcome_id[cmu$phone_count > phone_threshold]
long_probability <- length(long_entries) / nrow(cmu)

stopifnot(
  phone_threshold %in% cmu$phone_count,
  abs(long_probability - mean(cmu$phone_count > phone_threshold)) < 1e-12
)

c(threshold = phone_threshold,
  selected_entries = length(long_entries),
  empirical_probability = long_probability)
```

The empirical third quartile is `r phone_threshold` phones. The event above that threshold is

$$
\{\omega\in\Omega\mid X(\omega)>q_{.75}\},
$$

where $q_{.75}$ is computed in the displayed code. It contains `r format(length(long_entries), big.mark = ",")` pronunciation entries and has empirical probability `r sprintf("%.3f", long_probability)`. The event contains outcomes, not bare counts.

A [**random variable**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html) maps outcomes to values. A probability statement about values denotes the corresponding event in the original outcome space. The [next page](defining-random-variables.qmd) makes this correspondence precise with preimages and measurability.

## One outcome can support several questions

The same pronunciation can satisfy both $X(\omega)=x$ and $V(\omega)=v$. The two mappings do not compete because they encode different questions about the same represented entry.

This separation matters because a stored linguistic record is usually richer than any one response. Keeping the outcome identifier, orthographic form, and phone sequence lets a later analysis study alternate pronunciations or particular phone patterns. Replacing the entry with its count would remove those possibilities.

## Check your understanding

1. Use `cmu` to list the entries in the event $V=1$. Why are the entries, rather than the number one, the event members?
2. Define a random variable that maps a pronunciation entry to its number of consonant phones. Verify from the data that $X=V+C$ for every entry.
3. Change `phone_threshold` to the empirical median. How many outcomes belong to the resulting upper-tail event?
4. Which information is lost if `phone_count` replaces the complete pronunciation-entry record?
5. Why would dividing each word's empirical mass equally across its alternate
   pronunciations define a different probability experiment?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The event $V=1$ contains the 16,935 pronunciation-entry rows with one vowel phone; the rows are members because an event is a subset of outcomes, while one is the mapped value. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Defining $C(\omega)$ as the consonant-phone count gives `all(cmu$phone_count == cmu$vowel_phone_count + cmu$consonant_phone_count)`, so $X=V+C$ for every entry. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The empirical median is 6 phones, and the strict upper-tail event $X>6$ contains 56,478 outcomes. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Replacing the full record with `phone_count` loses word identity, pronunciation identity and sequence, stress information, and the vowel–consonant composition. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. Uniform row sampling gives every pronunciation entry equal mass. Assigning
   equal word mass first and then splitting that mass among variants changes
   the outcome weights, especially for words with several entries.

</details>

An outcome is a full pronunciation entry, while a random variable maps that
entry to a value. An event stated in terms of those values is nevertheless a
set of entries. The next page formalizes that last step with a preimage.
